summary: The note describes the tools and techniques used to forecast space weather, prompted by a September 15, 2023 geomagnetic storm that disrupted power and communications. It covers satellites, ground-based observatories, computer models, real-time analytics, machine learning, international collaboration, public education and visual tools. Experts such as Dr. Emily Zhao and Dr. Frank Barnes stress that forecasting remains difficult because of the sun's dynamic behavior, even as investment in the technology grows.
one_line: Overview of satellites, observatories, models, AI and global collaboration used to forecast space weather after the September 15, 2023 geomagnetic storm outages.
key_facts: On September 15, 2023, large swaths of the globe experienced power disruptions and interrupted communication services due to an unexpected geomagnetic storm.
Space weather includes solar flares, geomagnetic storms, and coronal mass ejections (CMEs), which can harm power grids, satellites, and communications.
Dr. Emily Zhao, lead astrophysicist at the National Space Weather Program (NSWP), said on September 18, 2023 that the sun's energy bursts can hit Earth within minutes to days.
Some satellites sit at the Lagrange point between the Earth and the sun, such as the Deep Space Climate Observatory (DSCOVR), providing real-time data on solar winds and solar imagery.
Dr. Frank Barnes, satellite operations manager, explained the role of satellite observatories on October 22, 2023.
Ground-based facilities like the Global Oscillation Network Group (GONG) and neutron monitors detect early signs of solar activity and measure high-energy particles reaching Earth's atmosphere.
The Wang-Sheeley-Arge (WSA)-Enlil solar wind prediction model uses satellite data to simulate the sun's atmosphere and predict the arrival of CMEs.
The Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) uses sophisticated algorithms and real-time analytics; data scientist Dr. Liam Richards spoke on this at a seminar on November 3, 2023.
Machine learning models are trained on historical solar event data so they improve their predictions over time, according to Dr. Richards.
The Community Coordinated Modeling Center (CCMC) facilitates worldwide collaboration; Dr. Maria Fernández of the European Space Agency stressed international partnerships on December 5, 2023.
Dr. Zhao emphasizes educational outreach to electric power operators, airlines, and anyone dependent on GPS navigation.
The NSWP and similar agencies use charts, graphs, and 3D models to turn complex data into actionable information.
Investment in forecasting technology is rising, with new programs and satellites designed to improve detection and response times.
Predicting space weather remains challenging because the sun's dynamic behavior can cause rapid changes.
